lessons.title: Bonjour l'art!
lessons.oneGoal: Students will recognize art exists everywhere around them

mindsOn.activity: Circle time greeting with art objects. Show 3-4 familiar items (crayon, picture book, decorated pencil case). Point and say 'Voici l'art!' Use big gestures and excited voice. Students repeat with actions.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Large word cards with pictures: ART (paintbrush icon), VOIR (eye icon), COULEUR (rainbow)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students seem confused by French: Use more gestures, point to their eyes when saying 'voir', hold up colorful objects for 'couleur'. If they're engaged: Add simple questions like 'Où est l'art?' (Where is art?)

activities: Art Hunt Walk (~9 min): Walk around classroom/school. Stop at artwork, colorful displays, decorated doors. Point and say 'Je vois l'art!' Students echo with pointing gesture.
Color Treasure Hunt (~9 min): Students find objects of specific colors you call out in French. 'Trouvez du rouge!' Hold up color cards. Celebrate finds with 'Bravo! C'est l'art!'
My Art Collection (~9 min): Each student chooses one art object from hunt. Sit in circle. Show object saying 'Mon art!' Others respond 'Bonjour art!' with wave gesture.
action.visualSupport: Color cards held high, pointing gestures for 'voir', heart hands for 'mon art'
action.decisionPoint: If students lose focus during walks: Stop for 30-second dance break, use call-and-response chants. If they're too excited: Use whisper voice and calm gestures to model quiet observation.

consolidation.activity: Art Gallery Share. Students place their chosen art object on desk. Walk around like in an art gallery, whispering 'Je vois...' and naming colors they see. End with group cheer: 'L'art est partout!' (Art is everywhere!)
consolidation.assessment: Can students point to art when asked 'Où est l'art?' Can they repeat 'voir' with eye gesture? Do they recognize 'couleur' with color objects?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are still energetic: Extend gallery walk with quiet background music. If they're tired: Sit for sharing instead of walking, use thumbs up for 'J'aime l'art!'

lessons.emergencyBackup: Picture book art hunt: Use any picture book, point to illustrations saying 'Voici l'art!' Students find colors and repeat vocabulary. Works with any adult, no French required.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Looking for art in their bedroom, kitchen, playground - send home simple visual checklist with pictures

lessons.title: Mes yeux découvrent
lessons.oneGoal: Students will use their eyes to observe details in their environment

mindsOn.activity: Review game with Lesson 1 vocabulary using actions. Then introduce 'regarder' with exaggerated looking gesture (hand above eyes like binoculars). Practice looking at ceiling, floor, each other with 'Je regarde...'
mindsOn.visualSupport: Previous lesson word cards plus new cards: REGARDER (binocular hands icon), DÉTAIL (magnifying glass), FORME (circle, square, triangle shapes)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students remember Lesson 1 well: Move quickly through review and focus on new vocabulary. If they need more practice: Spend extra time on 'voir' vs 'regarder' distinction with clear gestures.

activities: Detective Eyes (~9 min): Use magnifying glasses (real or pretend hands). Look closely at classroom art from Lesson 1. Point out details: 'Je regarde le détail!' Students copy detective posture and whisper discoveries.
Shape Hunt (~9 min): Search environment for basic shapes (circle, square, triangle). When found, trace shape in air saying 'Une forme!' Use shape cards to match discoveries.
Detail Drawing (~9 min): Choose one art piece/object. Students draw ONE detail they noticed (just simple lines/shapes). Share by pointing to detail on drawing: 'Mon détail!'
action.visualSupport: Large shape posters on walls, teacher demonstrates tracing shapes in air, point to eyes frequently when saying 'regarder'
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with fine details: Focus on obvious features like big shapes or bright colors. If they're ready for more challenge: Introduce texture words like 'lisse' (smooth) with touch gestures.

consolidation.activity: Detail Gallery Walk. Post drawings on board. Students walk by and point to details they can identify, saying 'Je vois un détail!' or 'Une forme!' End with group celebration of their detective eyes.
consolidation.assessment: Can students demonstrate 'regarder' with appropriate gesture? Do they point to shapes when asked 'Où est la forme?' Can they identify at least one detail in artwork?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to share more: Allow extra time for pointing and celebrating discoveries. If they're restless: Turn into movement game where they find shapes with their bodies.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Shape puppet show: Use any geometric shapes (blocks, cut paper). Make shapes 'talk' to each other in simple French. Students identify and respond to shapes. No art background needed.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Noticing shapes in clouds, patterns on clothing, textures on playground - encourage 'detective eyes' at home and recess

lessons.title: J'aime, j'aime pas
lessons.oneGoal: Students will express simple preferences about visual things they see

mindsOn.activity: Show two contrasting art pieces (bright vs dark, busy vs simple). Model preferences with clear gestures: 'J'aime!' (thumbs up, smile) and 'J'aime pas!' (gentle shake of head). Students practice with hand gestures for each phrase.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Word cards: J'AIME (smiley face, thumbs up), BEAU (heart, beautiful object), PRÉFÉRER (pointing finger choosing between two options)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students hesitate to express dislikes: Emphasize that different opinions are good, use 'J'aime mieux...' (I like better). If they're very vocal: Channel energy into structured turn-taking with talking stick.

activities: Opinion Gallery (~9 min): Post 6-8 different art images around room. Students walk with partners, stopping to whisper 'J'aime' or 'J'aime pas' with gestures. No judgment, just sharing preferences quietly.
Beautiful Hunt (~9 min): Students search classroom for something 'beau' (beautiful). Bring back to circle, show and say 'C'est beau!' Others can agree 'Oui, c'est beau!' or respectfully disagree.

Choose Your Favorite (~9 min): Present two similar art pieces. Students vote by moving to preferred side of room. Count votes in French, celebrate that both sides have supporters: 'Bravo! Nous préférons différents!'
materials: Two easels or wall spaces for voting activity
action.visualSupport: Consistent use of thumbs up/down gestures, heart hands for 'beau', pointing gesture for choice-making
action.decisionPoint: If students all copy each other's choices: Model independent thinking by saying 'Mon opinion est...' If some students don't participate: Pair with confident buddy or allow observation without pressure.

consolidation.activity: Preference Circle. Students sit with their 'beau' object from hunt. Each shares: 'J'aime...' and points to their object. Others respond with 'C'est beau!' End with 'Nos goûts sont différents!' (Our tastes are different!)
consolidation.assessment: Can students use 'j'aime' with appropriate gesture? Do they attempt 'beau' when shown beautiful objects? Can they make a choice when presented with options?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If sharing takes too long: Limit to pointing and saying vocabulary without explanations. If students want to elaborate: Allow extra French phrases or drawing their feelings.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Picture book preferences: Use any picture book with varied illustrations. Point to different pages asking 'J'aime ou j'aime pas?' Students show thumbs up/down. Celebrate all answers as valid opinions.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Choosing favorite toys, clothes, or foods based on how they look - encourage family conversations about preferences

lessons.title: Mes mains créent
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore basic art materials safely and confidently

mindsOn.activity: Hand warm-up with finger wiggles and 'magic hands' gestures. Introduce vocabulary with TPR: hold up 'crayon' and pretend to draw, wave 'papier' like a flag, use both hands in creating motion for 'créer'. Students mirror all actions.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Real objects with word cards: CRAYON (crayon drawing), PAPIER (paper sheets), CRÉER (hands making something, magic sparkles)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are very excited about materials: Start with clear handling expectations through demonstration. If they seem nervous about creating: Emphasize exploration over perfection, 'Pas de problème!'

activities: Material Exploration (~9 min): Students handle different crayons and papers. Practice vocabulary by holding up items and saying words. Try different pressures and motions: 'Je crée avec le crayon!'
Paper Play (~9 min): Explore different types of paper (smooth, textured, colored). Feel with hands, try drawing on each type. Use French: 'Mon papier est...' with gesture descriptions.
Creation Time (~9 min): Free creation with chosen materials. Focus on process, not product. Circulate saying 'Tu crées!' (You're creating!) Students can respond 'Je crée!' with proud gesture.
materials: Simple smocks or paper towels for cleanup
action.visualSupport: Teacher demonstrates each material use, vocabulary cards displayed at material stations, hand gestures for 'créer'
action.decisionPoint: If students focus too much on 'perfect' drawings: Redirect to exploring materials and processes. If they finish quickly: Encourage trying different tools or helping organize materials.

consolidation.activity: Creator Circle. Students hold their creation and share: 'J'ai créé avec...' (holding up their crayon type). Others celebrate: 'Bravo! Tu crées!' Practice putting materials away properly saying 'Merci, crayon!' to each tool.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify 'crayon' and 'papier' when shown? Do they attempt 'créer' with creation gestures? Are they handling materials appropriately and safely?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If cleanup takes too long: Turn into sorting game with French counting. If students want to continue creating: Promise more creation time next lesson, save unfinished work carefully.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Paper sculpture: Use any paper available. Show simple folding, rolling, tearing techniques. Students experiment saying 'Je crée' with each action. No drawing skills needed, focus on manipulation.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Drawing pictures for family, decorating their room, making cards - encourage trying different papers and crayons at home

lessons.title: Lignes partout!
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create different types of lines with purpose

mindsOn.activity: Body lines: Students make straight lines with arms ('droite' - arms out straight), curved lines with bodies ('courbe' - bend and sway). Draw lines in air following teacher. Use whole body to understand 'ligne' concept with movement.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Large line examples on board: LIGNE (various line types), DROITE (ruler, straight fence), COURBE (snake, rainbow, smile)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students struggle with straight vs curved concept: Use familiar objects (ruler vs smile) and body positions. If they grasp it quickly: Add descriptive words like 'zigzag' with arm movements.

activities: Line Hunt (~9 min): Search classroom for straight and curved lines. Point and identify: 'Une ligne droite!' (door frame) or 'Une ligne courbe!' (clock face). Students trace found lines with finger in air.
Line Dancing (~9 min): Move bodies to create line types. Walk straight paths for 'droite', curved paths for 'courbe'. Draw lines on ground with feet, in air with whole arms.
Line Art (~9 min): Create artwork using only lines. Students choose to focus on straight lines, curved lines, or mix both. Emphasize that lines can show feelings: happy curves, strong straights.
action.visualSupport: Teacher draws large examples on board, uses arm/body gestures for each line type, points to found lines during hunt
action.decisionPoint: If students make only scribbles: Guide focus to one line type at a time, demonstrate control. If they're very controlled: Encourage bigger movements, whole-arm drawing for expression.

consolidation.activity: Line Gallery. Post artwork at student eye level. Walk gallery style, students point to different line types they see: 'Je vois une ligne droite!' Celebrate variety and effort with specific praise about line choices.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify straight vs curved lines when pointed out? Do they attempt to create intentional line types? Can they use body movements to show line concepts?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to add to their line art: Allow quick additions but maintain focus on lines only. If they're tired from standing: Do gallery walk sitting on floor, passing artwork around circle.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Finger line tracing: Use any textbook or worksheet with printed lines (letters, borders, pictures). Students trace over lines with fingers, identifying 'droite' or 'courbe'. Requires no art supplies.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Lines in sidewalk cracks, tree branches, their own hair - notice and name line types during outdoor play and daily routines

lessons.title: Formes magiques
lessons.oneGoal: Students will recognize and create basic shapes in art

mindsOn.activity: Shape actions: Draw shapes in air while saying names. 'Cercle' - arms make big circle, 'carré' - four-cornered gesture with index fingers, 'triangle' - three-pointed shape with arms above head. Students mirror and chant shape names.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Large colorful shape cutouts: CERCLE (ball, wheel, sun), CARRÉ (window, book, gift box), TRIANGLE (hat, slice of pizza, mountain)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students confuse shapes: Focus on one shape at a time with multiple examples and clear body gestures. If they know shapes well: Introduce French pronunciation emphasis and add 'la forme est...' sentence structure.

activities: Shape Detective (~9 min): Search environment for shapes. Students call out discoveries: 'Un cercle!' (clock) 'Un carré!' (window). Keep tally chart of found shapes, celebrate finds with shape gesture.
Shape Building (~9 min): Use shape templates or free-hand drawing to create large versions of each shape. Students work in pairs, one draws while other gives encouragement: 'C'est un bon cercle!'
Magic Shape Art (~9 min): Create simple pictures using only one shape type repeated (circle flowers, square robots, triangle trees). Focus on seeing possibilities within limitations.
materials: Chart paper and markers for tally
Crayons and paper for individual work
action.visualSupport: Shape reference charts on walls, teacher demonstrates drawing each shape slowly, hand gestures for each shape consistently used
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with shape drawing: Provide templates or dotted outlines to trace. If they're artistically ambitious: Encourage shape combinations but maintain vocabulary focus.

consolidation.activity: Shape Gallery Share. Students display their magic shape art and identify what shapes they used: 'J'ai utilisé des cercles!' (I used circles!) Others guess what they see in the shape art: 'Je vois un soleil!' (I see a sun!)
consolidation.assessment: Can students name shapes when shown? Do they recognize shapes in environment when prompted? Can they create recognizable versions of basic shapes?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to elaborate on their shape art: Encourage simple French descriptions using known vocabulary. If sharing takes too long: Use simultaneous partner sharing instead of whole group.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Shape sorting: Use any classroom manipulatives (blocks, books, supplies). Sort into shape categories while practicing French names. Students take turns being 'shape caller' - no drawing required.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Shapes in their house windows, food, toys, and books - family shape hunting game at home with simple checklist

lessons.title: Couleurs vivantes
lessons.oneGoal: Students will use color intentionally to express ideas

mindsOn.activity: Color energy movement: 'Rouge' - stomp like fire, 'bleu' - flow like water, 'jaune' - bounce like sunshine. Students mirror movements while chanting color names. Show how colors can have personalities and feelings.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Pure color cards with associations: ROUGE (fire, apple, stop sign), BLEU (sky, water, sadness), JAUNE (sun, happy face, banana)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students get overly excited with movements: Use quieter 'color breathing' - inhale red energy, exhale blue calmness. If they seem restrained: Encourage bigger movements and vocal color calls.

activities: Color Hunt Plus (~9 min): Find objects in primary colors, but add emotional connection: 'Le rouge me fait sentir...' (Red makes me feel...). Students show emotions through face and body when finding colors.
Color Mixing Magic (~9 min): Explore what happens when primary colors meet. Use paint or colored transparent sheets. Students predict and discover: 'Rouge et jaune font...' (Red and yellow make...)

Intentional Color Art (~9 min): Create artwork choosing colors for specific reasons: happy picture uses yellow, calm picture uses blue, exciting picture uses red. Students explain choices: 'J'utilise le bleu parce que...' (I use blue because...)
action.visualSupport: Color emotion chart displayed, teacher demonstrates mixing with excited commentary, color words repeated with consistent actions
action.decisionPoint: If color mixing gets messy: Simplify to colored pencil layering or transparent sheets. If students want to mix more colors: Focus on discoveries but maintain primary color vocabulary.

consolidation.activity: Color Intention Share. Students explain their color choices: 'J'ai choisi le rouge pour...' (I chose red for...). Others listen and respond with color connections: 'Le rouge me fait penser à...' (Red makes me think of...)
consolidation.assessment: Can students name primary colors in French? Do they make intentional color choices? Can they explain their choices using simple French phrases?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If explanations become too complex: Simplify to color + emotion words only. If students are very engaged: Allow extra time for color discovery and sharing observations.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Color story: Tell simple story using only color words and gestures. Students act out different colors as characters. 'Rouge was angry, Bleu was sad, Jaune came to make everyone happy!' No art supplies needed.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Colors in nature, their favorite foods, seasonal changes - discuss how colors make them feel in different situations at home

lessons.title: Textures à toucher
lessons.oneGoal: Students will explore how texture can be shown in art

mindsOn.activity: Texture box mystery: Without looking, students feel objects of different textures. Describe with actions: 'doux' - gentle pet motion, 'rugueux' - scratchy clawing motion, 'toucher' - reaching out with fingertips. Guess and reveal objects.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Texture cards with touch demonstrations: TOUCHER (hand reaching out), DOUX (feather, kitten, silk), RUGUEUX (sandpaper, bark, rock)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are squeamish about touching unknown objects: Use familiar classroom items and let them see first. If they're very tactile: Provide more texture variety and encourage detailed descriptions.

activities: Texture Exploration Station (~9 min): Set up texture samples (sandpaper, cotton, fabric, foil). Students move between stations touching and practicing vocabulary: 'C'est doux!' or 'C'est rugueux!'

Texture Art Techniques (~9 min): Learn to create texture in drawings: press crayons hard for rough, gentle strokes for smooth, use side of crayon for different effects. Students experiment with textural drawing techniques.

Texture Picture (~9 min): Draw something that has both smooth and rough parts (tree with smooth leaves, rough bark). Focus on showing texture differences through artistic techniques, not just coloring.
materials: Texture sample collection (sandpaper, cotton, fabric, bubble wrap)
action.visualSupport: Texture demonstration board showing drawing techniques, consistent hand gestures for texture words, real texture samples visible
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with showing texture in drawings: Focus on feeling real textures first, then simple techniques. If they're artistically advanced: Introduce more sophisticated textural drawing methods.

consolidation.activity: Texture Gallery Walk. Students touch each other's texture artwork (gently!) and identify what they feel: 'Je touche... c'est doux!' Partner discussions about texture choices and techniques used.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify smooth vs rough textures by touch? Do they attempt to create textural effects in their art? Can they use 'toucher', 'doux', 'rugueux' appropriately?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students are too rough with artwork: Demonstrate gentle touching and establish gallery rules. If they want to add more textures: Allow experimentation with other materials if time permits.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Classroom texture hunt: Find smooth and rough surfaces around room (desk tops, carpet, walls). Students touch and categorize using French texture words. No art supplies needed, just exploration.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Feeling bark on trees, smooth stones, fuzzy sweaters - encourage texture awareness during outdoor play and daily activities

lessons.title: Mes sentiments en art
lessons.oneGoal: Students will connect their emotions to their artistic choices

mindsOn.activity: Emotion mirror: Teacher shows emotion faces and students mirror while saying French words. 'Content' - big smile and relaxed shoulders, 'triste' - sad face and drooping posture, 'excité' - bouncy energy and wide eyes. Practice transitioning between emotions.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Emotion face cards: CONTENT (happy face, calm colors), TRISTE (sad face, drooping elements), EXCITÉ (surprised face, energetic lines and bright colors)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are uncomfortable showing emotions: Start with just facial expressions, no pressure to share personal feelings. If they're very expressive: Channel energy into artistic choices rather than dramatic displays.

activities: Emotion Art Gallery (~9 min): Show artwork examples that convey emotions (happy bright paintings, sad dark ones, excited energetic ones). Students identify: 'Cette image est...' and explain what makes them think so.
Feeling Colors (~9 min): Experiment with color choices for emotions. What colors show 'content'? 'Triste'? 'Excité'? Students create small color samples for each emotion with brief explanations.

My Feeling Art (~9 min): Students choose current emotion and create artwork to match. Focus on color and line choices that express their feeling. Emphasize that all feelings are valid and can make beautiful art.
action.visualSupport: Emotion art examples posted around room, color-emotion chart created together, consistent emotion gestures and faces
action.decisionPoint: If students all choose same emotion: Encourage variety by discussing different situations that create emotions. If someone chooses difficult emotions: Support with appropriate artistic expression without prying.

consolidation.activity: Emotion Art Share. Students hold artwork and share their emotion choice: 'Mon art montre que je suis content!' Others respond supportively: 'Je comprends ton sentiment!' (I understand your feeling!)
consolidation.assessment: Can students name emotions in French? Do they make artistic choices that connect to emotions? Can they identify emotions in artwork?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If sharing becomes too personal: Keep focus on artistic choices rather than personal reasons. If students want to share more: Allow extra time but maintain supportive, non-judgmental atmosphere.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Emotion charades: Students act out emotions while others guess in French. Then discuss what colors or lines might show those emotions. No art supplies needed, focus on expression and vocabulary.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Happy birthday drawings, comfort objects, celebrating achievements - encourage expressing feelings through art at home during different moods

lessons.title: Outils d'artiste
lessons.oneGoal: Students will select appropriate tools for their artistic intentions

mindsOn.activity: Tool parade: Hold up each tool type with exaggerated demonstration. 'Pinceau' - painting gestures in air, 'colle' - sticky finger motions, 'ciseaux' - cutting actions (safety emphasis). Students practice motions while chanting tool names.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Real tools with word cards: PINCEAU (paintbrush with paint drops), COLLE (glue bottle with sticky drops), CISEAUX (scissors with cut paper)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are overly excited about scissors: Establish safety rules immediately with demonstration. If they're nervous about new tools: Start with most familiar tool and build confidence gradually.

activities: Tool Exploration Stations (~9 min): Set up stations for each tool type. Students rotate, trying each tool with appropriate materials. Practice saying tool names while using: 'J'utilise le pinceau!'

Right Tool for the Job (~9 min): Present art challenges: 'How do we join two papers?' (colle), 'How do we make shapes from paper?' (ciseaux), 'How do we add paint?' (pinceau). Students match tools to tasks.

Multi-tool Creation (~9 min): Create artwork that requires all three tools. Plan steps: first cut shapes, then glue them, finally add painted details. Students practice tool vocabulary throughout process.
action.visualSupport: Tool demonstration poster showing proper use, safety reminders visible, teacher models each tool use clearly
action.decisionPoint: If tool management becomes chaotic: Limit to one tool at a time until routines are established. If students finish quickly: Encourage helping others or creating additional elements.

consolidation.activity: Artist Tool Talk. Students show their multi-tool artwork and explain which tools they used: 'J'ai utilisé les ciseaux pour...' Others ask questions: 'Pourquoi le pinceau?' Tool cleanup becomes vocabulary practice.
consolidation.assessment: Can students name art tools in French? Do they choose appropriate tools for specific tasks? Are they using tools safely and purposefully?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If cleanup takes too long: Make it a French counting and sorting game. If students want to continue creating: Promise more multi-tool projects, emphasize proper tool storage.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Tool pantomime: Students act out using different art tools while others guess in French. Discuss what each tool does best. No actual tools needed, focus on understanding tool purposes.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Choosing right tools for jobs at home, helping with crafts - encourage noticing when family members select specific tools for different tasks

lessons.title: Techniques nouvelles
lessons.oneGoal: Students will try new art techniques to achieve different effects

mindsOn.activity: Technique demonstrations: Show each new technique with exaggerated actions. 'Mélanger' - stirring/mixing motions, 'tamponner' - dabbing/stamping actions, 'gratter' - gentle scratching movements. Students practice motions in air while learning pronunciation.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Technique demonstration cards: MÉLANGER (swirling colors together), TAMPONNER (sponge dabbing pattern), GRATTER (scratch art revealing colors underneath)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students want to rush into techniques: Demonstrate each one slowly first, emphasizing control over speed. If they're hesitant to try new things: Start with most familiar technique and build confidence.

activities: Technique Stations (~9 min): Set up three stations - mixing colors (mélanger), sponge painting (tamponner), crayon scratch art (gratter). Students rotate and try each technique with guided practice.

Technique Comparison (~9 min): Students create three small samples, one for each technique. Compare effects: 'Le mélange fait...' 'Le tamponnage crée...' 'Le grattage montre...' Discuss which they prefer for different purposes.

Technique Choice Art (~9 min): Students choose one technique to create larger artwork. Focus on exploring the chosen technique thoroughly rather than trying to use all three. Encourage experimentation and discovery.
action.visualSupport: Step-by-step technique posters at each station, teacher circulates demonstrating techniques, vocabulary cards visible at each station
action.decisionPoint: If one technique is too popular: Encourage trying others by showing different effects possible. If techniques are too difficult: Simplify steps or provide more guidance at challenging stations.

consolidation.activity: Technique Gallery. Students explain which technique they chose and why: 'J'ai préféré mélanger parce que...' Others observe technique effects in different artworks. Celebrate variety of choices and discoveries made.
consolidation.assessment: Can students name techniques in French? Do they attempt new techniques willingly? Can they identify technique effects in artwork?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to try more techniques: Note interest for future lessons, focus on mastering current ones. If some struggled with techniques: Pair with successful peers for next technique practice.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Technique storytelling: Tell story of three artist friends who each had special technique. Students act out techniques while story progresses. No art supplies needed, focus on understanding and movement.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Different ways to spread jam, clean windows, or play in sand - connect art techniques to daily activities that use similar motions

lessons.title: Mon style unique
lessons.oneGoal: Students will recognize their own artistic preferences and style

mindsOn.activity: Style celebration: Look at student artwork from previous lessons. Point out different approaches: 'Voici le style de...' Emphasize that different is wonderful. Students practice saying 'Mon style est unique!' with proud gestures.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Student artwork examples showing variety, word cards: STYLE (different artistic approaches), UNIQUE (one-of-a-kind symbol), SPÉCIAL (star, crown, heart)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students compare themselves negatively: Emphasize that every style has special qualities, avoid comparative language. If they're not seeing differences: Point out specific style elements in their work.

activities: Style Detective (~9 min): Look at several student artworks together (anonymous). Identify style differences: bold vs gentle lines, bright vs soft colors, detailed vs simple approaches. Practice vocabulary: 'Ce style est spécial!'
My Style Portfolio (~9 min): Students choose 3-4 pieces of their own work from previous lessons. Arrange them to show their style consistency. Look for patterns in their choices and approaches.

Style Statement Art (~9 min): Create new artwork that represents their personal style. Students make intentional choices about colors, lines, techniques based on their preferences discovered in portfolio review.
action.visualSupport: Style comparison charts showing different artistic approaches, positive vocabulary for describing styles, examples of famous artist styles
action.decisionPoint: If students can't see their own style: Help point out consistent choices they've made. If they want to copy others: Encourage appreciation while maintaining individual expression.

consolidation.activity: Style Celebration Circle. Students share one thing that makes their style special: 'Mon style est spécial parce que...' Others respond with appreciation: 'Ton style est unique!' End with group cheer about everyone being special artists.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify style differences in artwork? Do they recognize their own artistic preferences? Can they use vocabulary to describe uniqueness positively?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If sharing becomes competitive: Redirect to appreciation and individual celebration. If students are very engaged: Allow extra time for peer appreciation and style observations.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Style dress-up: Students describe their clothing style choices using French vocabulary. Connect to artistic style: 'My clothes are bright like my art!' No art supplies needed, personal connection.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Their unique way of decorating, dressing, or arranging their space - encourage family conversations about what makes each person special

lessons.title: Partager mes idées
lessons.oneGoal: Students will communicate about their art using French vocabulary learned

mindsOn.activity: Communication practice: Teacher models different ways to share art. 'Expliquer' - pointing and describing, 'montrer' - displaying and indicating features, 'raconter' - telling story about the art. Students practice each gesture style.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Communication cards: EXPLIQUER (person pointing and talking), MONTRER (hands displaying/presenting), RACONTER (storytelling gestures)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are shy about sharing: Start with partner sharing before whole group. If they're very talkative: Provide sentence starters to focus communication.

activities: Art Interview (~9 min): Students work in pairs, taking turns being artist and interviewer. Interviewer asks: 'Peux-tu expliquer ton art?' Artist practices using previous vocabulary to describe their work.

Gallery Guide Practice (~9 min): Students choose one artwork to 'guide' others through. Practice presentation skills: 'Je vais vous montrer...' Focus on clear communication using learned French art vocabulary.

Art Story Time (~9 min): Students create simple stories about their artwork: 'Je vais raconter l'histoire de mon art...' Encourage imagination and use of descriptive vocabulary from all previous lessons.
action.visualSupport: Sentence starter charts posted, communication gesture reminders, vocabulary word walls from all previous lessons available
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with French communication: Allow gesture and simple words, focus on attempting communication over perfection. If they're very fluent: Encourage more complex descriptions and peer questions.

consolidation.activity: Communication Celebration. Students vote for different communication awards: 'Meilleure explication' (best explanation), 'Meilleure histoire' (best story), 'Meilleure présentation' (best presentation). Everyone gets recognized for something special.
consolidation.assessment: Can students attempt to explain their art in French? Do they use learned vocabulary in communication? Are they comfortable sharing their artistic ideas?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to continue sharing: Note enthusiasm for future presentation opportunities. If some didn't present: Ensure they get opportunity in smaller setting later.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Show and tell circle: Students simply show artwork and say one French word about it. Others repeat the word and clap. Focus on vocabulary reinforcement over complex communication.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Showing family their creations, explaining their room decorations - encourage practicing French art words when sharing at home

lessons.title: Art dans ma vie
lessons.oneGoal: Students will demonstrate understanding of how art connects to their daily experience

mindsOn.activity: Daily art hunt: Students think about their morning routine and identify art they saw/used: clothing patterns, cereal box designs, toothbrush colors. Practice vocabulary: 'L'art est important dans ma vie quotidienne!' (Art is important in my daily life!)
mindsOn.visualSupport: Daily life art examples: IMPORTANT (special symbol, heart), QUOTIDIEN (calendar, daily routine pictures), UTILISER (hands using/holding objects)
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students don't see art in daily life: Provide specific examples from classroom and help them make connections. If they see art everywhere: Channel enthusiasm into organized sharing and vocabulary practice.

activities: Art Life Map (~9 min): Students draw simple map of their day, marking where they see or use art: bedroom decorations, breakfast dishes, school supplies, playground equipment. Label with French vocabulary.

Art Importance Discussion (~9 min): Talk about why art matters in daily life. Students share: 'L'art est important parce que...' Focus on personal connections and emotional responses to everyday visual elements.

Using Art Plan (~9 min): Students plan how they will use art in their life going forward. Draw or write simple goals: 'Je vais utiliser l'art pour...' (I will use art to...) - decorate, express, create, notice.
action.visualSupport: Sample daily life art map, importance discussion prompts visible, vocabulary cards for expressing plans and goals
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle to see art connections: Provide concrete examples and help make personal links. If they're overwhelmed by art everywhere: Help focus on most meaningful connections.

consolidation.activity: Art Life Commitment. Students share one way they will use art in their daily life: 'L'art va être important dans ma vie parce que...' Create class commitment to noticing and creating art every day.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify art in daily life? Do they understand why art is important? Can they express plans for using art vocabulary appropriately?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students need more concrete examples: Focus on immediate classroom and home connections. If they're making abstract connections: Celebrate sophisticated thinking while maintaining vocabulary focus.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Art gratitude circle: Students say 'Merci' to different art elements in the classroom, explaining why: 'Merci, couleurs, parce que vous me rendez heureux!' Focus on appreciation and vocabulary.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Making art part of their daily routine, noticing design everywhere - encourage family discussions about art in their home and community

lessons.title: Atelier libre
lessons.oneGoal: Students will practice all learned techniques in self-directed creation

mindsOn.activity: Art vocabulary review game: Students take turns acting out vocabulary words from lessons 1-14 while others guess in French. Quick energy builder that reinforces all learned terms before independent work time.
mindsOn.visualSupport: All vocabulary cards from previous lessons displayed around room for reference during independent work
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students need vocabulary review: Spend more time on key terms they'll use during free studio. If they remember well: Move quickly to planning their independent art projects.

activities: Project Planning (~5 min): Students choose what type of art to create using any combination of learned techniques. Brief planning: What materials? What techniques? What colors? What style?

Independent Creation (~17 min): Students work on self-chosen projects. Teacher circulates, asking questions in French: 'Pourquoi cette couleur?' 'Quelle technique utilises-tu?' Encourage vocabulary use.
Peer Consultation (~5 min): Students can visit each other for feedback or help, practicing communication vocabulary: 'Peux-tu m'aider?' 'J'aime ton style!' Focus on supportive interaction.
materials: All art materials from previous lessons available
action.visualSupport: Technique reminder posters, vocabulary word walls, examples of student work from previous lessons for inspiration
action.decisionPoint: If students struggle with independence: Provide more structure with specific project choices. If they're very independent: Allow advanced exploration while maintaining French vocabulary focus.

consolidation.activity: Artist Reflection. Students complete sentence starters: 'Aujourd'hui j'ai utilisé...' (Today I used...) 'Ma technique préférée était...' (My favorite technique was...) 'Je suis fier de...' (I'm proud of...)
consolidation.assessment: Are students choosing techniques purposefully? Do they use French vocabulary naturally during creation? Can they work independently while applying learned skills?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to continue working: Note projects for next lesson completion. If they're satisfied with work: Focus on reflection and vocabulary reinforcement.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Free choice art using only available classroom supplies (pencils, paper, classroom decorations for inspiration). Focus on creativity and vocabulary use rather than specific materials.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Having art time at home, making gifts, decorating personal spaces - encourage establishing regular creative time in daily routine

lessons.title: Collaboration artistique
lessons.oneGoal: Students will work together on artistic projects using learned vocabulary

mindsOn.activity: Collaboration warm-up: Partner mirror drawing - one student draws while partner mirrors movements in air. Practice sharing materials and space. Introduce collaboration phrases: 'On peut partager?' (Can we share?) 'Bonne idée!' (Good idea!)
mindsOn.visualSupport: Collaboration phrase cards and gesture reminders, examples of collaborative art projects
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students struggle with sharing: Start with individual materials that can be traded. If they collaborate naturally: Introduce more complex group project structures.

activities: Partner Art Creation (~12 min): Students work in pairs on single artwork, taking turns adding elements. Must communicate in French: 'Je vais ajouter...' (I'm going to add...) 'Qu'est-ce que tu penses?' (What do you think?)

Small Group Mural (~15 min): Groups of 3-4 create section of class mural. Each student responsible for different element (background, foreground, details, colors) while coordinating with group members.
action.visualSupport: Collaboration vocabulary posted, examples of successful group artwork, clear workspace organization
action.decisionPoint: If conflicts arise over artistic choices: Introduce compromise vocabulary and decision-making strategies. If collaboration flows smoothly: Add more complex collaborative challenges.

consolidation.activity: Collaboration Celebration. Groups present their collaborative work, explaining how they worked together: 'Nous avons collaboré en...' (We collaborated by...) Others appreciate: 'Votre collaboration est belle!' (Your collaboration is beautiful!)
consolidation.assessment: Are students sharing materials and space appropriately? Do they communicate about artistic decisions? Can they compromise and build on each other's ideas?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to continue collaborative work: Plan future group projects. If some preferred individual work: Balance collaboration with independent options in future lessons.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Collaborative storytelling: Students take turns adding to visual story on board using simple drawings while practicing French vocabulary. No individual supplies needed.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Making art with siblings, friends, or family members - encourage collaborative creative projects at home

lessons.title: Art en grand
lessons.oneGoal: Students will apply their skills to larger-scale creative projects

mindsOn.activity: Scale exploration: Compare small and large versions of same artwork. Discuss challenges and opportunities of working big: 'En grand, je peux...' (When working big, I can...) Practice big gestures and movements for large-scale art.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Examples of small vs large artwork, gesture cards showing big movements and techniques
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students seem overwhelmed by scale: Start with medium-sized projects and build up. If they're excited about big projects: Channel energy into planning and technique consideration.

activities: Large Format Exploration (~10 min): Students experiment with making big marks, bold colors, sweeping movements on large paper. Practice techniques adapted for scale: 'Pour travailler en grand, j'utilise...' (To work big, I use...)
Big Project Planning (~7 min): Students plan larger artwork considering: What techniques work best big? How to organize large space? What tools are needed? Simple sketching and material selection.
Large Scale Creation (~10 min): Students begin larger projects, focusing on adapting learned techniques to bigger format. Emphasis on process and problem-solving rather than completion.
materials: Large format paper (poster size or larger)
Floor space or large table areas
action.visualSupport: Technique adaptation charts showing small vs large methods, workspace organization examples, tool selection guides
action.decisionPoint: If large format is too challenging: Allow medium-sized projects with focus on scale principles. If students adapt easily: Introduce more complex large-scale techniques.

consolidation.activity: Scale Reflection. Students compare their large-scale work experience with smaller projects: 'Travailler en grand était...' (Working big was...) 'J'ai appris que...' (I learned that...) Discuss challenges and successes.
consolidation.assessment: Can students adapt techniques to larger formats? Do they plan appropriately for scale? Are they problem-solving when challenges arise?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If projects are unfinished: Plan continuation time and storage solutions. If students are satisfied: Focus on reflection and skill transfer to other contexts.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Floor art: Use chalk or washable markers on floor tiles (if available) to create large-scale temporary art. Focus on big movements and scale adaptation.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Decorating their bedroom, making posters, creating gifts for family - encourage thinking about scale in home projects

lessons.title: Galerie de classe
lessons.oneGoal: Students will curate and present their artwork in a gallery setting

mindsOn.activity: Gallery visit preparation: Discuss how art galleries work. Practice gallery behavior: quiet voices, careful looking, respectful comments. Introduce curatorial vocabulary: 'Je choisis cette œuvre parce que...' (I choose this work because...)
mindsOn.visualSupport: Gallery behavior reminder cards, curatorial decision-making prompts, examples of art gallery layouts
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students are unfamiliar with galleries: Spend more time on gallery etiquette and purpose. If they know galleries: Focus on curatorial decision-making skills.

activities: Artwork Selection (~8 min): Students choose 2-3 pieces from their collection to display. Must justify choices: 'J'ai choisi ceci parce que...' Focus on quality, variety, or personal meaning.

Gallery Setup (~10 min): Students help arrange classroom gallery, considering how artwork looks together, viewing angles, and flow through space. Practice presentation vocabulary: 'Cette œuvre montre...' (This work shows...)

Gallery Opening (~9 min): Students take turns being gallery visitors and artists. Artists present their work briefly, visitors ask respectful questions and offer appreciative comments using learned vocabulary.
materials: All student artwork from previous lessons
action.visualSupport: Gallery layout examples, presentation sentence starters, visitor question prompts
action.decisionPoint: If setup takes too long: Simplify display methods and focus on presentation skills. If students are natural curators: Allow more complex exhibition decision-making.

consolidation.activity: Gallery Reflection. Students complete gallery visitor forms: 'Mon œuvre préférée était...' (My favorite work was...) 'J'ai appris...' (I learned...) 'La galerie m'a fait sentir...' (The gallery made me feel...)
consolidation.assessment: Can students make thoughtful curatorial choices? Do they present their work confidently? Can they engage respectfully as gallery visitors?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want extended gallery time: Leave display up for other classes to visit. If they're ready to move on: Focus on reflection and skills learned through curation.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Desk gallery: Each student creates mini gallery on their desk with 2-3 small artworks. Others visit desk galleries in small groups, practicing vocabulary and respectful viewing.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Displaying their art at home, choosing what to show to visitors - encourage creating personal art displays in their rooms

lessons.title: Art et nature
lessons.oneGoal: Students will create art inspired by natural elements and materials

mindsOn.activity: Nature art exploration: Show examples of natural materials used in art (leaf printing, stone painting, twig sculptures). Discuss respectful collection: 'Nous prenons seulement ce que nous avons besoin' (We take only what we need). Practice nature vocabulary review.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Examples of nature art, collection guidelines with pictures, review of nature-related vocabulary from previous lessons
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If outdoor collection isn't possible: Use pre-collected natural materials or nature photographs. If weather permits: Plan brief outdoor collection time with clear guidelines.

activities: Natural Material Collection (~8 min): If possible, brief outdoor time to respectfully collect leaves, small stones, twigs. If indoor: explore pre-collected materials. Practice descriptive vocabulary: 'Cette feuille est...' (This leaf is...)

Nature Art Techniques (~10 min): Explore different ways to use natural materials in art: printing, rubbing, arranging, incorporating into drawings. Students experiment with techniques using French vocabulary: 'Je crée avec...' (I create with...)

Nature-Inspired Creation (~9 min): Students create artwork either using natural materials directly or drawing/painting inspired by natural forms. Focus on connecting to previous lessons' vocabulary and techniques.
action.visualSupport: Nature art technique examples, vocabulary cards for natural materials, connection charts linking nature to previous art concepts
action.decisionPoint: If natural materials are limited: Focus on nature-inspired drawing and painting. If materials are abundant: Allow more experimentation with direct natural material incorporation.

consolidation.activity: Nature Art Share. Students present their nature art explaining their inspiration: 'La nature m'inspire parce que...' (Nature inspires me because...) 'J'ai utilisé...' (I used...) Connect to environmental appreciation.
consolidation.assessment: Can students work respectfully with natural materials? Do they connect nature inspiration to artistic techniques? Can they explain their nature-art connections in French?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If students want to collect more materials: Plan future nature art sessions with proper guidelines. If they prefer other inspirations: Validate preferences while celebrating nature connections made.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Nature drawing from observation: Use any plants visible from classroom windows or indoor plants. Students practice observational drawing while using descriptive vocabulary.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Collecting leaves and flowers, rock painting, nature photography - encourage respectful nature appreciation and creation at home

lessons.title: Célébration artistique
lessons.oneGoal: Students will celebrate their artistic growth and share with families

mindsOn.activity: Growth reflection: Students look through portfolio of work from all lessons. Identify improvements and new skills: 'Au début, je...' (At the beginning, I...) 'Maintenant, je peux...' (Now I can...) Celebrate progress with encouraging gestures.
mindsOn.visualSupport: Portfolio organization from all 20 lessons, growth reflection prompts, celebration vocabulary and gestures
mindsOn.decisionPoint: If students don't see their own growth: Point out specific improvements and skill development. If they're very proud: Channel pride into sharing preparation and goal-setting for future.

activities: Portfolio Preparation (~10 min): Students organize their best work and practice explaining their artistic journey: 'Mon art préféré est...' (My favorite art is...) 'J'ai appris à...' (I learned to...) Prepare for family sharing.

Celebration Art Creation (~12 min): Students create special celebratory artwork that shows their current skills and style. Can incorporate favorite techniques, colors, and approaches from all lessons.
Sharing Practice (~5 min): Students practice presenting their portfolio and celebration art, using all learned vocabulary confidently. Focus on pride in growth and continued artistic goals.
action.visualSupport: Portfolio organization examples, presentation practice prompts, vocabulary summary from all lessons available for reference
action.decisionPoint: If students are nervous about family sharing: Focus on peer sharing and portfolio pride. If they're excited to share: Prepare special presentation format and celebration atmosphere.

consolidation.activity: Artist Commitment Circle. Students share one artistic goal for the future: 'Je veux continuer à...' (I want to continue to...) 'L'art va toujours être important parce que...' (Art will always be important because...) Group celebration of artistic growth.
consolidation.assessment: Can students identify their artistic growth? Do they use learned vocabulary confidently? Are they excited about continuing artistic development?
consolidation.decisionPoint: If family sharing is planned: Focus on preparation and confidence-building. If this is final celebration: Emphasize achievement recognition and continued art appreciation.

lessons.emergencyBackup: Art appreciation circle: Students take turns appreciating something special about each classmate's artistic development using French vocabulary. Focus on community celebration and individual recognition.
lessons.realWorldConnection: Continuing to make art at home, noticing art everywhere, sharing creativity - encourage lifelong artistic engagement and French vocabulary use
